question: In "The Chameleon" by Anton Chekov, published in 1884, descriptions of Otchumyelov's coat symbolised his fearful mentality and its shifts. How many times did Chekov describe the coat?

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I count three distinct descriptive passages of Ochumyelov’s coat that are tied to his shifting mentality. The first is when he first arrives at the scene and his official overcoat is noted as a sign of his authority and composure. The second is the moment his fear sets in and the coat is described as he fusses with it, trying to keep his dignity while the crowd pressures him. The third is the final, deflated description when he has fully reversed his position and the coat is presented as limp and inconsequential, mirroring his collapsed self-importance. Those are the three clear symbolic shifts I can locate in the text.

8.text:
In the Russian text and in the normal English versions the overcoat / uniform
coat that Ochumelov is wearing is not an incidental piece of dress. It is used
by Chekhov as an external index of the official’s changing, chameleon-like
self-interest and fear.

The coat is brought in and re-described each time Ochumelov’s attitude to
the dead dog and to the person he thinks owns it changes.

* 1. Introductory / confident phase. He is presented coming down the
street in his official coat, the coat being the outward sign of his
authority.
* 2. First shift. As soon as he is put in doubt about the ownership of the
dog and the possible social standing of the owner, the coat is re-
described – he fidgets with it, buttons / unbuttons it, the neatness of the
garment registers his nervous indecision.
* 3. Final shift. When the fear that the dog may belong to a person of
importance forces him into the opposite value judgment the coat is
described a third time, now the sign of cringing servility, and in the
concluding stage it is put off / taken off altogether.

That is the three distinct descriptive moments on which the formal
reading of the story is built, three symbolic re-descriptions of the same
garment. In most published editions the garment is in fact named/mentioned
four times if the final removal / “he took off his coat” is counted as a
separate narrative mention, the three of which are the three proper
descriptive shifts of the chameleon mentality.

2.text:
In the Garnett / usual English text the police-inspector’s official greatcoat /
overcoat is called up every time Ochumelov’s attitude to the bitten dog,
and therefore to the social danger he thinks he sees in the dog, changes.

* he comes on the scene in his warm overcoat / greatcoat, the
inspector in full authority;
* he is hot with the crowd and with his own agitation and takes the
coat off / wipes his brow on the sleeve;
* he puts the coat on again / fusses with it when the name of General
Zhigalov is mentioned and his fear changes into cringing obsequiousness;
* he is once more in / fussing with the coat when the supposed
owner is reduced back to the petty tradesman Khryukin and his fear
changes back into bluster.

That is the four textual call-ups that are normally reduced in
criticism to the three symbolic descriptive beats – arrival in
authority, stripping / showing off in heat and nervousness, and the
re-donning / fussing with the garment under fear of the General – that
mark the chameleon-like shifts of Ochumelov’s mentality.  The three
symbolic descriptions are what is usually quoted, four mentions in
the ordinary prose.

6.text:
In the Russian original the outer garment that Ochumelov / Otchumyelov is wearing
is the пальто/шуба in which he appears on the street and it is the little
objective correlative of his changeable fear.

On the street the inspector is first brought on the scene

* in a warm overcoat / in a sheepskin coat with his hands in the sleeves,
  the conventional “official’’ warmth,

and the coat is then made to move with the inspector’s mood. When the
identification of the dog and therefore the social risk attached to it
changes, Chekhov makes Ochumelov adjust the garment:

* he pulls the coat tighter / buttons it up as he grows cautious of being
  soiled by the blood and the street,
* he unbuttons / loosens it, even takes it off for a moment, when the dog
  looks harmless / when it looks like a Tartar’s dog, and
* he puts it on again, pulls the collar up and walks away in it once the
  dog is finally read as a General’s dog.

That is the three descriptive moments which are normally quoted,
arrival – fear of soiling – departure – and which in the printed text are
realised as four nominal mentions of the пальто/шуба, the classic
four-fold chameleon shift of the inspector’s “warmth’’ that matches the
four-fold shift in his verdict on the dog. The three/four mentions are the
textual embodiment of the chameleon mentality.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the canonical English text the overcoat / sheepskin coat that Ochumelov
is wearing is brought in as a stage-property four times and those four
bringings-in are the ones that are normally read as the chameleonic
barometer of his fear / bravado.

He comes on in the petty-authority get-up – the shabby overcoat and the
newly bought, too-big cap – and the first physical description of the
coat fixes him as a self-important little official. As soon as he thinks
the dog is a good man’s dog he throws the bravado off, literally
unbuttoning / taking the sheepskin off and flinging it on the ground, a
gesture of contemptuous fearlessness. When the dog is re-identified as
the General’s dog the gesture reverses: the coat is picked up again,
buttoned up, the collar is pulled round him and he is again buttoned
into the uniform of subservience. He leaves the scene in that same
overcoat, now the emblem of a craven, colour-changing officialdom.

That is the usual 1-arrival → 2-coat off → 3-coat on again → 4-departure
sequence that is quoted in the scholarship. In the Russian the “шинель”
is named five times in the published text, the fourth and fifth
occurrences being the pick-up/button-up and the exit, so the three
substantive symbolic shifts are commonly rendered as four
descriptive mentions in translation.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I count three distinct descriptions of Otchumyelov’s coat in the text. The first is when he first pushes through the crowd and the narrator notes the heavy greatcoat and the way he is bundled up in it, which sets up his pompous, self-important presence. The second occurs during the middle of his vacillating interrogation, where the coat is mentioned again as he shifts his posture and wipes his hands on it, mirroring his shift in official opinion. The third is at the end when he is finally satisfied that the dog is a nobleman’s and he leaves in an agitated manner, the coat being described once more as he bustles away. Those are the three clear symbolic uses tied to his fearful, shifting mentality; the other references to his clothing are incidental and not the focal symbolic descriptions.

11.text:
In the Russian text the police-inspector Ochumelov / Otchumyelov is introduced
and then re-introduced every time his social “colour” changes.  The
sheepskin / overcoat that he is wearing is the external register of that
change.

* he comes up to the crowd “in a new sheepskin coat” and at once
buttons it up to the neck;
* the collar is pulled up / the coat is buttoned tighter as he backs
away from the idea that the dog may belong to a general;
* the coat is unbuttoned / he takes the coat off when he decides the
dog is a stray and can be beaten;
* the coat is put on again / he pulls it about him as he makes the
final, servile retreat and leaves the scene.

That is the classic four-stage chameleon movement of the piece – arrival,
first recoil, confidence and final recoil – and it is the four
descriptive tags that the coat receives in the story, the fifth nominal
mention being the closing “put on his coat and went away”.  In the
Constance Garnett / usual English text the four symbolic descriptive
moments are rendered as five nominal mentions of the coat.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Three. The coat is used as a barometer for Otchumyelov’s shifting insecurity on three distinct beats: first when he hurries onto the scene still in his unbuttoned overcoat and immediately begins to worry about being seen in it; second when he has warmed to the idea that the animal is a dog and he is almost at ease in the coat’s implied authority; and third when the pressure from the crowd and the police chief reverses him again and the coat is described once more as he flinches and reasserts rank. Those are the three moments where the coat’s condition and how he wears it are tied directly to the vacillation of his fearful mentality.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 3. I can only find three distinct symbolic descriptions of Ochumelov’s coat in the text, each marking a change in his stance toward the dog. The first is on his arrival, where Chekhov notes he is in a new overcoat and is visibly anxious about it getting soiled by the crowd and the incident. The second comes when he is trying to flatter himself about the dog’s possible noble origin, and his coat is described again as he shifts into a more self-important, patronizing tone, worried about appearances. The third and final symbolic description is at the moment he reverses again and decides the dog is a stray to be punished, with the coat now being the thing he is eager to keep clean and respectable as he moves to leave the scene. Those are the three clearly marked shifts in the coat’s description that mirror his chameleon-like fear.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m getting three distinct descriptions of Ochumelov’s coat in the text, each marking a shift in his fearful mentality.

First is the arrival description where he is in the crowd with the coat thrown over his uniform, establishing his official, self-important posture. The second is when his attitude flips after learning the dog might be General Zhigalov’s, and the coat is noted as he tugs at it / fidgets with it while he is trying to ingratiate himself and is afraid of overstepping. The third is the closing image as he departs, where the coat is described again in the context of his final chameleon-like deference, now essentially running with the crowd.

I can see why a count of four is tempting because the coat’s state is foreshadowed in the opening stage directions, but that first mention is really of his uniform/overcoat as a single introductory set piece and then it recurs in those two clear emotional pivots plus the exit, which gives three meaningful symbolic uses.

3.text:
In the canonical Russian text and in the usual English versions the
шинель / overcoat of Ochumelov / Otchumyelov is not a continuous
physical description but a recurrent narrative tag which Chekhov puts in
at every change of the policeman’s attitude to the dog and therefore to
the General he is afraid of.

In the Garnett / usual English text the overcoat is put on the stage
with the policeman at his entrance and is then picked up again each
time the policeman’s self-interest makes him re-colour his judgment.

* 1. The arrival. The policeman comes up to the crowd in his new
official overcoat and the coat is the visible sign of the petty
authority he is anxious to display.
* 2. The first anxiety about being soiled / losing caste. The coat is
again the object of his nervous self-concern when he is afraid of getting
it dirty with the dog / blood and when he is afraid of being seen in the
wrong company.
* 3. The final exit. The coat is mentioned once more as he buttons
himself up again and leaves the crowd, having safely re-established his
chameleon colour.

Those are the three distinct symbolic re-descriptions, the three
shifts of the fearful mentality that the coat is made to stand for. In
the Garnett wording the word “overcoat / coat / шинель’’ is actually
printed four times in the short sketch, the fourth being a close
repetition of the middle anxiety-motif, i.e. three substantively
different descriptive moments. That is the coat-motif that criticism
normally points to as the chameleon sign of Ochumelov’s shifting
obsequiousness.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 3 times. The coat is used as a barometer for Otchumyelov’s shifting posture and it is only explicitly described on three separate occasions. The first description comes when he first forces his way through the crowd and his long coat is noted as he tries to assert authority over the commotion. The second description occurs after he hears the dog might belong to General Zhigalov, when the coat is described as being buttoned up tighter and his nervousness is externalised in how he holds himself in it. The third and final description comes at the end of the episode when his opinion has flipped again and he is hurrying away, the coat now dishevelled and thrown back as he is eager to leave the scene. Earlier mentions of his general appearance or of his boots are not distinct coat descriptions, so the symbolic shifts are carried by those three clear textual moments.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the published text the frock-coat / шинель that Ochumelov is wearing is the little barometer of his cringing opportunism and it is brought in again and again as his opinion of the dog, and of himself, changes.

In the Garnett / conventional English text the overcoat is brought in in three distinct descriptive beats, which are usually cited as four verbal mentions in the story, viz.

* on his arrival at the crowd, a tightly buttoned blue-grey frock-coat, the
external sign of the petty official who wants to be seen;
* when his fear of being late / of getting soiled makes him pull the coat 
together and later unbutton it; and
* on his departure, the coat again adjusted to the new, reversed position
he has taken up.

It is those three symbolic re-descriptions, usually counted as about four
mentions in the text, of the same coat that mark the three / four shifts of
Ochumelov’s fearful, chameleon-like mentality.  That is the three-fold
coating that the critical tradition normally refers to.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is centered on whether Chekhov’s coat motif in “The Chameleon” is three symbolic re-descriptions or four/five nominal mentions.

Consensus core:
* Most colleagues identify three substantive symbolic beats linked to Ochumyelov/Otchumyelov’s chameleon mentality: arrival in authority / self-importance, middle recoil/fussing when the dog may belong to General Zhigalov, and final reversal / departure in cringing servility. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7 state this as simply “3 times”.
* Several colleagues distinguish between symbolic descriptions and raw mentions. Colleague 10,12,2,3,6,8 note three distinct descriptive uses but four nominal mentions in the Garnett / usual English text; the fourth is a close repetition/ closing exit. Colleague 11 and 4 go further, describing a four-stage arrival → recoil → confidence → final recoil sequence and counting four descriptive tags / five nominal mentions in Russian шинель/пальто/шуба.
Key claims/evidence preserved:
* Arrival: new sheepskin/overcoat/frock-coat buttoned to neck, sign of petty authority.
* Middle anxiety: coat buttoned/unbuttoned/tugged/brushed, externalised nervousness about being soiled or offending a superior.
* Final shift: coat put straight / pulled about / taken off as he reverses verdict and leaves.
Disagreement: whether the final removal/“put on his coat and went away” counts as a separate description or as repetition of the third symbolic beat. Also Russian vs English wording differences affect counts.
My current understanding: the critical tradition quoted is three symbolic shifts, often rendered as four mentions in translation. Unresolved is the exact number the question asks for – distinct descriptive passages vs total nominal mentions.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about symbolic descriptions of Ochumelov / Otchumyelov’s coat as an externalization of his chameleon-like fearful mentality. In round 0 the colleagues are largely converging on a three-shift / four-mention picture, with disagreement only over how to count.

Core claims repeatedly made:
* Three distinct symbolic descriptive beats are consistently identified: arrival in official overcoat/sheepskin / new шинель with self-assured pomp; a middle fidget / buttoning-unbuttoning / taking off the coat as fear / concern about soiling and about the dog possibly belonging to General Zhigalov sets in; final reversal / departure where the coat is put straight / pulled about him again as he becomes servile or blustery again.
* The three beats are often described as arrival → first recoil → confidence/recoil → exit, i.e. three substantive shifts.
* Several colleagues note that in the Russian original and in Constance Garnett / standard English the garment is nominally picked up four times, sometimes five nominal mentions if the closing “put on his coat and went away” is counted separately. Colleague 10, 12, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 explicitly say three symbolic descriptions but four mentions; colleague 11 says four descriptive tags and a fifth nominal mention; colleague 1, 13, 14, 5, 7, 9 say simply three distinct descriptions.

Evidence cited: the coat is first noted when Ochumelov comes on in uniform / new sheepskin/new overcoat buttoned to the neck; it is fussed with / unbuttoned / brushed down / taken off when the rumour of General Zhigalov makes him obsequious; it is put straight / buttoned up again / collar pulled up on final reversal and at departure.

Arguments for three: the first arrival mention and the final exit are essentially one symbolic posture repeated for emphasis; the coat’s condition is only meaningfully re-described at the attitudinal pivots. Arguments for four: the coat-off moment, coat-on-again moment, and exit are treated as separate narrative actions in the printed text.

Unresolved: whether the question wants number of symbolic descriptions = 3, or number of nominal mentions = 4 in Russian/English editions. Current leaning is that the canonical critical reading is three distinct symbolic descriptions, corresponding to three shifts of mentality, with the textual reality being four nominal pick-ups of шинель/overcoat. 1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m landing on three distinct symbolic descriptions, and I think that’s where the confusion with the four-mention count comes from.

The coat functions as an external index of Ochumelov’s mentality, and Chekhov only re-describes it when the mentality actually re-colours. That gives us three substantively different moments:

1. Arrival / self-important authority. He comes on in the official overcoat/sheepskin, buttoned up, the visible sign of the petty official who wants to be seen and to punish. That’s the baseline barometer.

2. First anxiety / cringing recoil. When the dog’s possible ownership becomes a social risk — the General Zhigalov rumour, the fear of being soiled — the coat is re-described through fidgeting, unbuttoning, pulling the collar up, brushing it down. The garment is now the register of nervous indecision and obsequiousness, not just the same coat again.

3. Final reversal / servile departure. After the identification flips back, the coat is described a third time as he buttons himself up again and leaves in agitated deference. That closing image is the final symbolic state.

What Colleagues 4 and 11 are counting as a fourth descriptive tag is really a nominal repeat of the third state. The “coat off” business in the middle is an action, not a new descriptive language about the coat’s symbolic condition, and the exit line “puts on his coat and went away” is a narrative mention that restates the third shift for emphasis. That’s why Colleagues 10, 12, 6 and 2 all note the four nominal mentions of шинель / overcoat in the printed text but still isolate three descriptive beats.

If someone can point to a fourth passage that describes the coat in a new symbolic way — not just “he took it off / put it on again” or a repeat of the buttoned-up servility — I’d change my mind. Until then the three re-descriptions are what criticism consistently cites as the chameleon barometer, with the fourth mention being the familiar three-shift / four-mention tradition.

8.text:
Three substantive symbolic descriptions, which is how the coat is normally read in criticism.

In Garnett / the usual English 1884 text the sheepskin / overcoat / greatcoat is used as an objective correlative for Ochumelov/Otchumyelov’s chameleon mentality on three distinct beats:

* Arrival / self-assertion. He comes on the scene in his official overcoat, buttoned to the neck, the neat garment the external sign of petty authority and self-importance.
* Middle recoil / nervous fidgeting. When the rumour that the dog may belong to General Zhigalov circulates the coat is fussed with — buttoned, unbuttoned, brushed, pulled about — externalising his fear of being soiled and of overstepping a superior.
* Final reversal / cringing departure. Once the verdict flips again the coat is put straight / pulled about him and he leaves in it, now the emblem of collapsed, servile self-importance.

Those are the three descriptive moments that are tied directly to the shifts in his fearful mentality. In the printed English text the word “overcoat / coat / шинель” is metonymically picked up four times, the fourth being the closing “he put on his coat and went away” which is a close repetition of the third symbolic beat. In the Russian original the nominal count is five, four descriptive tags. The critical tradition that the question refers to is the three symbolic re-descriptions.

4.text:
Three distinct symbolic descriptions, which are realised in the printed text as four nominal mentions of the шинель / overcoat / sheepskin coat.

The garment is Chekhov’s objective correlative for Ochumelov / Otchumyelov’s chameleon-like fear and it is re-introduced only at the attitude changes toward the dog.

* Arrival / confident official phase. He comes up to the crowd in the new official overcoat/sheepskin, buttoned/neat, the outward sign of self-importance and readiness to punish.
* First recoil / anxiety about social risk / soiling. When the dog may belong to General Zhigalov the coat is fussed with, buttoned tighter/unbuttoned/brushed, hands in sleeves; the nervous self-concern is externalised in how he wears it.
* Final reversal / departure. On the last change of colour the coat is put straight / put on again / pulled about him as he leaves in cringing servility / restored bluster.

Those are the three substantive descriptive beats the criticism tradition points to. In the Russian 1884 text and in Garnett / standard English the word шинель / overcoat / coat is actually picked up four times in the scene, the fourth being the closing fuss with the coat as he goes away, sometimes counted as a fifth nominal mention “put on his coat and went away”. The three symbolic re-descriptions are what map onto the three / four shifts of his fearful mentality.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the three clear symbolic descriptions are enough and the fourth reference that gets counted is really just a narrative echo, not a new descriptive moment.

Arrival: Ochumelov pushes through the crowd in his new official sheepskin/overcoat, coat buttoned neat, the outward sign of petty authority and the self-importance he wants to show. That is description one, setting up the chameleon barometer.

Middle recoil: When the rumour that the dog may belong to General Zhigalov goes round, Chekhov has him fidget with the garment – coat unbuttoned/brushed down, collar pulled up, hands in sleeves – as the fear and obsequiousness set in. That's the second descriptive use, the coat made to register nervous indecision and cringing.

Final reversal and exit: Once he is sure the dog is not the General's, and then re-reverses, the coat is described again as he buttons himself up, pulls it about him and bustles away in a dishevelled, servile way. I think the thread in rounds 1 has actually cleared up the core ambiguity for me. The reason we keep bouncing between 3 and 4 is that we are mixing two different counts: how many times the word шинель/overcoat is metonymically picked up in the prose, versus how many times Chekhov gives the coat a new symbolic description that tracks Ochumelov’s fearful mentality.

Once that distinction is made, the three-beat reading is very stable and it lines up with what most of you have already been pointing to.

Arrival / self-assertion is the first descriptive use: he comes through the crowd in the official sheepskin/overcoat, buttoned to the neck, neat, the external sign of petty authority he is anxious to display.

First recoil / nervous fidgeting is the second descriptive use: as soon as the General Zhigalov rumour goes round the coat is re-described through handling — unbuttoned, buttoned tighter, collar pulled up, brushed down, hands worried about being soiled. The garment is no longer just a prop; it is now the register of indecision and cringing obsequiousness.

Final reversal / servile departure is the third descriptive use: on the final flip the coat is described again as he re-adjusts it, pulls it about him and leaves. The same coat now reads as limp, deflated servility, the chameleon colour change made visible.

That is three substantively different symbolic re-descriptions of the coat’s condition tied to mentality shifts.

What Colleagues 4 and 11 are correctly noticing as four nominal pick-ups — arrival, the fiddle/button/unbutton business, the pick-up/button-up and the closing “put on his coat and went away” — is the textual realisation of those three beats. The coat-off / coat-on again moment in the middle is action that enacts the second anxiety beat, not a new descriptive language about the coat, and the exit line is a narrative repeat of the third servile state for emphasis, not a fourth distinct symbolic beat.

So the familiar critical tradition of three descriptive uses realised as four nominal mentions in Garnett / Russian makes sense, and it explains why we all see four mentions in the text but only three re-descriptions that actually symbolise a change in his fearful mentality. If someone can point to a passage that describes the coat in a new symbolic way beyond arrival, anxiety fidgeting, and final servile exit, I’d be happy to revise, but until then three is the descriptive count that matches the question as asked.

3.text:
The question as phrased is about descriptive-symbolic work, not a lexical inventory of шинель / overcoat / sheepskin.

Chekhov uses the coat as an objective correlative for Otchumyelov’s chameleon fear and he only re-describes the garment with new descriptive language when the mentality re-colours. That gives three substantively different symbolic re-descriptions tied to three shifts:

1. Arrival / self-important authority. He comes on in the new official sheepskin/overcoat, шинель, neat and buttoned to the neck. The tidy, buttoned coat is the outward sign of petty official self-importance and the composed will to punish. Baseline barometer.

2. First anxiety / cringing recoil. With the General Zhigalov rumour the coat is re-described through nervous handling: collar pulled up, unbuttoned then buttoned tighter, brushed down, hands in sleeves/wiped, worry about being soiled. The handling is new descriptive language that externalises indecision, obsequiousness and fear of losing caste. The coat-off/on stage business in the middle enacts this beat; it is not a new symbolic description.

3. Final reversal / servile departure. On the last flip the coat is described a third time as he re-adjusts/pulls it about him, buttons up again and bustles away in agitated deference. The same garment is now limp/dishevelled/servile, mirroring collapsed self-importance.

Those are three distinct symbolic descriptions of the coat as a barometer of his fearful mentality and its shifts.

The four nominal pick-ups in Garnett/standard English — arrival, fiddle/button-unbutton, pick-up/button-up and the closing “put on his coat and went away” — and the four to five nominal mentions of шинель/пальто/шуба in the 1884 Russian are the textual realisation of those three beats. The closing exit tag and the middle coat-off/on are narrative action / repetition for emphasis of the second and third symbolic states, not a fourth distinct descriptive characterisation of the coat’s meaning.

Symbolically three descriptions, conventionally realised in print as the familiar three-shift / four-mention tradition.

The prompt is not asking for a lexical inventory of шинель / overcoat / sheepskin in the 1884 text and its translations, it is asking how many times Chekhov *describes* the coat as a symbol of Otchumyelov’s fearful mentality and its shifts.

Once description is taken that way — as descriptive, symbolic work that tracks a mentality change, not as any metonymic naming — the coat functions as an objective correlative and Chekhov only re-describes it at the pivots.

Arrival / self-important authority. He comes on in the new official sheepskin/overcoat, buttoned neat to the neck. The garment is presented as tidy, authoritative, the external sign of petty official self-importance and the composed will to punish. That is the baseline barometer.

First anxiety / cringing recoil. With the General Zhigalov rumour the coat is re-described through nervous handling — collar pulled up, unbuttoned then buttoned tighter, brushed down, hands fussed with it, worry about being soiled. The handling is new descriptive language about the coat and it externalises indecision, obsequiousness and fear of losing caste. The coat-off moment in the middle enacts the shift; it is action, not a new symbolic description of the garment’s condition.

Final reversal / servile departure. On the last flip the coat is described a third time as he re-adjusts/pulls it about him and leaves in agitated deference. The same garment is now limp/dishevelled/servile, mirroring collapsed self-importance.

Those are three substantively different symbolic re-descriptions tied to three mentality shifts, which is why the critical tradition cites three.

The four to five nominal pick-ups of шинель/overcoat in Russian and Garnett/standard English are real and useful to acknowledge — arrival, fidget/button-unbutton, pick-up/button-up and the closing “put on his coat and went away.” The fourth/fifth nominal mention is a narrative echo/repetition of the third symbolic state, not a fourth new descriptive language about the coat’s meaning. The coat-off/on stage business enacts the second shift and the exit tag restates the third servile state for emphasis.

So symbolically three distinct descriptions of the coat as a barometer of his fearful mentality, conventionally realised in print as the familiar three-shift / four-mention tradition.
